newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan port workers step up U.S. sanction protest.
newsitem.headline: Japan port workers step up U.S. sanction protest.

text.p: Japanese port workers will refuse to work night shifts from March 31 in a stepped up protest against a U.S. decision to impose sanctions on Japanese ships calling at U.S. ports, union officials said on Tuesday.
The port workers, who are also calling for better working conditions, will not handle freight from 6 p.m. to 8 a.m (0900 GMT to 2300 GMT) for an indefinite period, officials said.
"We will not work night shifts until our demands are met," a union official said.
Operations at Japan's major ports, including Yokohama, Osaka, Tokyo, Kobe, Nagoya and Kanmon, will be disrupted and more ports are expected to join the action, the officials said.

The move by two major labour unions -- the National Council of Dock Workers' Unions and the Japan Confederation of Port and Transport Workers' Unions -- follows a 24-hour strike on March 12 which brought about 30 of Japan's 96 ports to a standstill.
The port workers have been angered by U.S. pressure to deregulate Japanese port practices, saying the changes sought by the United States would threaten their jobs.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission said on February 26 it would slap a $100,000 surcharge on each Japanese vessel entering a U.S. port from abroad from April 14 in retaliation for what Washington has called unfair Japanese port practices.

In response to the threat, Japan's Transport Ministry said earlier this month that a preliminary agreement had been reached between the Japan Harbour Transport Association and Japanese and foreign shipowners to reform certain Japanese port practices.
The association, made up of port cargo-handling firms, serves as an intermediary between unions and shipping companies.
Japanese officials are trying to set up a meeting with their U.S. counterparts before April 14, but have not yet settled on a date, a Foreign Ministry official said.
